abstract: There is an old Chinese proverb which says: ‘I hear, I forget I see, I remember I experience, I understand’ Virtual reality (VR) is rapidly growing in importance for business use. No longer relegated to the research lab, VR has the unique ability to give users the sensation and ‘experience’ of having gone through the computer screen to enter a computer-generated world. By using VR to improve understanding of complex 3-D data, companies are reporting significant benefits in cost savings, faster time-to-market and higher quality. VR is now poised to enter the business mainstream. IT professionals have an important role as the future implementors and integrators of VR systems. In this article, we shall be looking at the important trends and issues which are affecting companies, from an IT perspective, in trying to make the most of VR

Nothing competes with being there. Think of the experience of actually visiting a city like Venice or New York, compared to watching it on a video, or reading a travel book, or even using an interactive CD-ROM on a computer. Much as I am dedicated to my quad-speed CD-ROM, I have no doubt which experience I prefer. It is instructive to see an audience of children at a live entertainment event. Saturated as they are with big budget videos, wall-to-wall Saturday morning cartoons, and attention-intensive computer games, they still become totally engrossed with the live action on the stage and with the thrill of being there as it actually happens. So virtual reality is no substitute for real reality. Or is it?

The expansion of the world's financial markets has been phenomenal in recent years and it is no exaggeration to say that this would not have been possible without the widespread availability and use of IT. A visit to the trading floor of any major broker, with its interminable banks of computer screens will confirm this without question. This applies equally to almost every area of the markets from stock and commodity broking, through insurance and banking, to fund management and the very complex currency, futures and derivatives markets. Each is becoming ever more reliant upon IT in pursuit of efficiency and profit

What has happened to virtual reality in the past year? It has evolved substantially, as you might expect. But it has evolved in two very different ways, which has caused it to become different things to different people. To the public, VR has become synonymous with cyberspace, or surfing the Internet, while for the industrial/professional world, VR has become an innovative tool for improving operations and achieving greater profit

articleTitle: Weaving a stronger Web: not WWW but XXX
abstract: The World Wide Web and its HTML/HTTP protocol has changed the popular conception of the standards of visual presentation that can be achieved when transmitting information over networks. However, it is a mistake to assume that these standards are particularly good, or that the techniques used are particularly new. There is another protocol, with a long history behind it, which achieves more spectacular results and is capable of more sophisticated functions: the X windows protocol. X is the client-server system that is little known in the modern world of PCs - and is ignored by the Web

articleTitle: Seeking after the truth in computer evidence: any proof of ATM fraud?
abstract: ‘The revelation that Save & Prosper, the retail banking arm of Robert Fleming & Co, has been the victim of a £200,000 credit card fraud…shows how easy it can be to fool…card security systems. Details of customers’ cards were stolen and encoded on to other cards, such as those for petrol points. The bank suspected internal collusion after print-outs containing card details went missing, but an enquiry proved inconclusive. All affected customers have been reimbursed. Last month, it was revealed that £130,000 had been stolen from Abbey National cardholders during 1994 and 1995 with counterfeit cards. Andrew Stone, a bank security consultant who had been advising Which?, the magazine of the Consumers' Association, was jailed for five and a half years for the theft. This fraud involved spying on Abbey customers as they used their cards in automated teller machines (ATMs) or cash dispensers… [Stone] recorded card details and personal identification numbers (PINs) using powerful video cameras. The details were then encoded on the magnetic strips of other cards. Although all 500 victims were reimbursed by the bank, the stolen money has not been recovered… Such cases have highlighted yet again the serious issue of plastic card security…Card-issuers have been forced to admit that their security systems are not infallible and that ‘phantom’ withdrawals from ATMs are not always explained by the cardholder's negligence, or fraud by friends and relatives…’ From ‘Where the bucks stop’, Matthew Wall, Financial Times, October 19, 1996 ‘Experts agree…that technological failures account for only a tiny percentage of ATM losses’ From ‘Phantom withdrawals continue to haunt banks’, Financial Times, Alan Cane, September 21, 1996

articleTitle: Getting our act together: improving the national framework for ICT skills

articleTitle: BPR and OO: origins and common ground
abstract: This paper presents an analysis of two significant phenomena: business process re-engineering (BPR) and object orientation (OO). Each can be viewed as a modern day panacea for managers and IT specialists, respectively. We suggest a convergence which may help to address two major criticisms; of BPR that the reliance on often inflexible IT is dangerous; of OO that the approach helps programmers but doesn't ‘scale up’ to address real business problems by providing business objects to support business processes

Christmas 2007: a shopper looks longingly at a brightly packaged toy on a market stall. ‘Are you sure it's the only one you've got?’ he asks the trader. ‘Yeah - and if you want it, you'd better buy it now. These antiques sell in minutes.’ ‘My kid would love it,’ the shopper sighs. ‘OK. Do you take credit?’ ‘Sorry mate - cash only. The bank's down the street.’ The shopper realises two other customers are looking interestedly over his shoulder. ‘No, hold on a minute,’ he says, pulling out a mobile. He slots a card into the phone, dials the number of a bank, and taps a few other keys. ‘Mondex?’ he asks, taking out the card and handing it over. ‘That'll do nicely.’ The trader smiles. ‘The Gameboy's all yours.’

articleTitle: Whatever happened to hybrid managers?: The short history of the hybrids
abstract: As this last decade of the twentieth century was about to begin, it was predicted that hybrid managers would take us triumphantly into the new millennium, as the dynamic individuals who would realise - in both senses of the word - the full potential of IT. In 1990 Colin Palmer [1], Chairman of the British Computer Society Task Group on hybrid managers, wrote: ‘The (hybrid manager) term was coined by Michael Earl, Director of OXIIM at Templeton College, Oxford, as a result of a number of pieces of research that he and his colleagues had been undertaking. They noticed that in all the significant cases of successful implementation of information technology for competitive advantage or for achieving major change in organisations, there seemed to be a person at the heart of the development who displayed certain experience and characteristics. These were: an understanding of the business and what was required within the business, combined with a technical competence that enabled them to understand what was required in technical terms, including the scope of what was being planned. In addition to this, they displayed two types of organisational skills. They knew how to get about the business, and this implied that they knew the business and the people around it well, and they knew how to get things done, possessing a set of excellent social skills - to listen, understand, negotiate and persuade’

One might describe the many parts of the Service as being semi-autonomous and the level of IT expertise and IT penetration varies considerably between these parts. The STEP project aims to solve some of these problems

articleTitle: Digital's clusters and scientific parallel applications
abstract: Traditional implementations of message passing libraries such as PVM [1] have incurred high latencies. The use of a low latency interconnect [2] and well-tuned message passing software greatly reduces this latency. For an interesting class of applications, this reduced latency has a great impact on execution time. This article describes such a low latency interconnect, Memory Channel™, from a low-level programmer's perspective. It then gives an overview of the implementation of message passing libraries on top of Memory Channel, and finally describes the impact of such an optimized message passing facility on an application

On July 19 this year, two-thirds of the world's population focused on Atlanta, Georgia as the lighting of the Olympic flame marked the start of the 100th anniversary of the Modern Olympic Games. While the Olympic ideals haven't changed much in the intervening century, just about everything else has, including the challenges associated with managing the information technology necessary to stage today's Games.

articleTitle: VISION 2020: evolutionary solutions for managing corporate information
abstract: The development of relational database models and management systems (RDBMS) in the late 1960s and early 1970s first revolutionised and then denominated corporate data management for 25 years. They still do. I started this gaze into my VISION 2020 crystal ball with a respectful, if fleeting, glance back at this period, admitting at the outset that I was already a qualified accountant attending the very first Australian Computer Programmer's Course at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology well before RDBMS became king. In the course of my career, the asset value of information has grown exponentially every year, becoming a business in itself and a strategic factor in companies of every kind. Internal and external information flows are rapidly growing as the workplace becomes ever more computerised. Today, corporations have a critical need for systems which can handle all of their information, whether it exists as text, diagrams, images, audio or video information

articleTitle: WIZDOM for WINDOWS: simulating human thought processes
abstract: The use of object-oriented applications development is currently increasing and will surely influence the decisions regarding implementation strategies and software tool deployment during the remainder of this decade. Historically, the evolution of computer languages is divided into four generations: the first includes the binary languages, sequences of the bits; the second includes the assemblers; the third includes the highlevel languages, Cobol PL/1 etc.; the fourth includes the non-procedural languages and WYSIWYG. Could it be that the object-oriented (OO) methodology is the primary representative of the fifth generation?
